branches.description: Nerves, brains and the sense organs that feed them.
Gills, tracheae, lungs and air sacs.
Getting rid of waste and keeping water and salt in balance.
Eggs, larvae, wombs and growing up.
Bones, joints and muscles: the skeleton and how it moves.
Skin, scales, feathers, fur, colour and armour.

nodes.description: A diffuse web of neurons, like a jellyfish's.
Nerves bundled into cords along the body.
Nerve tissue gathers at the front, next to the senses.
Clusters of neurons in each segment that process signals locally.
Smell and taste: detecting dissolved chemicals.
Hundreds of lenses, each seeing a pixel: the eyes of trilobites and insects.
A hollow nerve cord along the back: the chordate spinal cord.
A lens focuses an image on the retina (vertebrates, cephalopods).
Forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain, each with its own jobs.
Extra-wide nerve fibres for lightning-fast escapes (squid).
Senses water movement along the flanks.
Insulated nerves carry signals far faster; first seen in jawed fish.
Coordinates movement and balance (jawed vertebrates).
Sense the faint electric fields of hidden prey.
A forebrain roof that combines the senses: the ancestor of the cortex.
Membranes that pick up sound in air.
More brain per kilo of body (early mammals and birds).
Six-layered cortex for flexible behaviour (mammals).
Hearing returning echoes of your own calls (bats, toothed whales).
Planning and self-control (great apes).
Body fluid is moved around by body movement and beating cilia.
A muscular tube that squeezes blood along.
Blood bathes the organs directly (arthropods, most molluscs).
Blood stays inside vessels and moves faster (annelids, vertebrates).
Copper-based blue blood that carries oxygen.
Iron-based red pigment that carries oxygen.
Haemoglobin packed into cells carries far more oxygen.
An atrium and a ventricle (fish).
Extra hearts pump blood through the gills (cephalopods).
Vessels one cell thick bring oxygen right up to every tissue.
Clotting proteins seal a wound before too much blood is lost.
Blood from the gut passes through the liver before reaching the body.
Two atria keep lung blood and body blood partly apart (amphibians).
The heart muscle gets a blood supply of its own, so it can work harder.
Extra pumps push blood into the wings, legs and antennae (insects).
Fully separate lung and body circuits (archosaurs, mammals).
Enough pressure to push blood up a sauropod's long neck.
Outgoing warm blood heats returning cold blood in flippers and legs.
On long dives the heart slows and blood goes to the brain (whales, seals).
Muscles packed with oxygen-storing myoglobin.
Oxygen diffuses in through a thin body wall.
Feathery surfaces for taking oxygen from water.
Slits in the throat that let water flow out past the gills.
Stacked gill plates (horseshoe crabs, sea scorpions).
Bony or cartilage arches support the gills.
Air tubes run straight to the tissues (insects, millipedes).
Closable openings to the tracheae that save water.
Air-breathing gill plates (scorpions, spiders).
A bony flap that pumps water over the gills.
Air sacs off the gut let fish gulp air in stagnant water.
The lung becomes a gas float for buoyancy (ray-finned fish).
Gulping air in with the floor of the mouth (amphibians).
A valve that guards the airway; later the voice box.
Expanding the ribcage to draw air in (amniotes).
A muscle sheet for powerful breathing (synapsids).
Scrolled nose bones that warm and moisten the air (warm-blooded animals).
Air flows one way through the lungs (dinosaurs, birds).
Breathing from a film of air held under water (water beetles).
The twin voice box of birds.
A folded chamber above the gills for breathing air (gouramis).
A sac with one opening, like a sea anemone's.
A mouth at one end and an anus at the other.
Mucus nets or gill rakers strain food from water.
A rasping tongue-ribbon (molluscs).
Biting jaws of arthropods.
Hinged jaws made from gill arches, so prey can be grabbed.
A muscular stomach that grinds food.
An acidic stomach digests large prey (jawed vertebrates).
Hard teeth for gripping and cutting.
A corkscrew intestine packs in more surface (sharks).
Lost teeth are replaced all through life (sharks, reptiles).
Microbes in an enlarged gut break down plant fibre.
Incisors, canines and molars for different jobs.
Glands that make venom, delivered by fangs, stings or grooved teeth (scorpions, centipedes, snakes).
A bony roof to the mouth: breathe while chewing.
Swallowed stones grind food (sauropods, birds).
A toothless keratin beak (turtles, birds, ceratopsians).
Molars that both slice and crush (mammals).
Hundreds of stacked teeth grind tough plants (hadrosaurs).
A many-chambered stomach for chewing the cud (ruminants).
Waste simply leaks out through the thin body wall.
Body fluids as salty as the sea, so there is no water balance to fight for (most marine invertebrates).
Paired tubules in each segment filter the body fluid (worms).
Beating cilia draw fluid into fine tubules (flatworms).
Toxic ammonia is flushed away with plenty of water: cheap in the sea.
Kidney-like glands at the base of the antennae (crustaceans).
The first vertebrate kidney: a few tubules just behind the head.
Kidneys filter waste out of the blood.
Tubules pull waste out of the body fluid into the gut (insects, spiders).
Cells in the gills pump salt in or out, for life in fresh or salt water.
A liver that breaks down poisons and worn-out blood for disposal.
Stores urine and lets water be taken back (tetrapods).
Ammonia is turned into urea, which is less toxic and needs less water (amphibians, sharks).
A gland that pumps out excess salt (sharks).
Almost every drop of water is recovered from the waste (desert beetles).
Water-saving solid waste (reptiles, birds, insects).
A compact kidney with many more filtering units (amniotes).
Glands that get rid of excess salt (marine reptiles, seabirds).
Concentrated urine saves water (mammals, birds).
Kidneys so efficient the animal never needs to drink (kangaroo rats).
Cells release chemical messages carried in body fluids.
Nerve cells that release hormones.
Hormones that control growth and the use of sugar.
Ecdysone decides when an arthropod moults.
The master gland under the brain.
Melatonin keeps track of day length and season.
Proteins that stop ice crystals forming in the blood.
Iodine hormones set the metabolic rate.
Adrenaline and cortisol: the fight-or-flight response.
Testosterone and oestrogen shape adult bodies.
Keeps insects as larvae until it is time to change.
A thyroid surge turns tadpoles into frogs.
Sleeping through droughts, like lungfish in mud cocoons.
Faster cells for sustained activity (therapsids).
The hormone behind brooding and milk.
Warm-blooded: body heat comes from metabolism.
A daily drop in body temperature to save energy.
Fat that burns to make heat.
The hormone of pair bonds and mother–young attachment.
Weeks-long deep torpor through the winter.
Releasing eggs and sperm into the sea.
Growing copies of yourself.
Drifting young that spread far.
Bigger eggs with stored food.
Regrowing lost body parts.
Sperm is delivered inside the female.
Sperm packets left for the female to pick up.
Females reproduce without males.
Fin organs for mating (sharks, placoderms).
Tough capsules that protect the embryo (mermaid's purses).
Tadpoles: amphibian young grow up in the water.
Young develop inside the mother (placoderms, ichthyosaurs).
An egg with its own membranes and water supply, so it can be laid on land.
Larva, pupa and adult (beetles, flies, butterflies).
Nest temperature decides the sex of the young (crocodiles, turtles).
Calcified shells (dinosaurs, birds).
Milk for the young.
The embryo is fed through the womb wall.
Tiny newborns finish growing in a pouch (marsupials).
Slow growth gives time for a bigger brain to develop.
A front, a back and two mirrored sides: the body plan of most animals.
Long and circular muscles for crawling, wriggling and burrowing.
The body is built from repeated segments that can specialise independently.
A fluid-filled cavity that cushions the organs and works as a hydrostatic skeleton.
A hard outer cuticle that protects the body and anchors the muscles.
Hinged legs inside the exoskeleton: the arthropod toolkit.
A stiff, flexible rod along the back: the first chordate skeleton.
Zig-zag muscle blocks that bend the body from side to side: fish-style swimming.
Blocks of cartilage or bone protect the nerve cord and stiffen the back.
A broad tail turns side-to-side bending into thrust.
Fins on both sides give steering, braking and lift.
Bone that replaces cartilage: the inner skeleton of bony fish and their descendants.
Legs that hold the body up out of water: the first land millipedes.
Fleshy fins with a bony core, the starting point for legs.
Fingers and toes at the end of the limb (Acanthostega had eight).
Shoulder and hip girdles strong enough to carry the body out of water.
Thin outgrowths of the thorax: the first animals to fly.
Legs held under the body for efficient running and breathing.
Air-filled bones are light and strong (dinosaurs, pterosaurs, birds).
Arms lined with flight feathers, as on Archaeopteryx.
Wandering cells that engulf bacteria and debris.
Small proteins that punch holes in bacteria.
Receptors that recognise molecules common to many microbes.
Parasites too big to swallow are walled off inside a capsule of cells.
Blood proteins that tag invaders and burst them open.
Invaders are smothered in melanin (insects, crustaceans).
Heat, swelling and a rush of defender cells to a wound.
An adaptive immune system of its own, built from different genes (lampreys, hagfish).
Lymphocytes reshuffle their genes to recognise almost any invader (jawed vertebrates).
Y-shaped proteins that lock on to one particular invader.
A gland where T cells learn to tell self from foreign.
Molecules that show fragments of invaders to T cells.
Filters the blood and stores immune cells.
Vessels that return fluid and carry immune cells.
A second infection is beaten faster than the first.
Blood and immune cells are made inside the bones (tetrapods).
Raising body temperature to slow down pathogens.
Mothers pass their protection on through the egg or milk.
Filter stations where immune cells meet invaders (mammals).
Antibodies are fine-tuned to fit their target better and better (mammals).
A protective outer layer of cells.
Slippery slime that protects the skin and eases movement.
A tough skin made of a sugar polymer.
Sharp projections deter predators (Wiwaxia, Hallucigenia).
Pigment cells that can change colour.
Bony plates in the skin (early jawless fish).
Tiny tooth-like scales that cut drag (sharks).
Making light with a chemical reaction.
A wax layer stops the body drying out on land.
Skin glands that make poison (amphibians).
Dry, waterproof scales (reptiles).
Bony plates under the scales (crocodiles, ankylosaurs).
Fuzzy filaments for insulation.
Insulating hair and skin glands (mammals).
Vaned feathers for warmth, display and flight.
Iridescent colour from microscopic structure instead of pigment.
Keratin-sheathed bony horns (ceratopsians, later antelopes and cattle).
Cooling by evaporation.
A thick fat layer insulates in cold seas.
Hairs hardened into spines (porcupines, hedgehogs).
Bright colours that advertise poison.
Dark above and pale below, so the body looks flat.
A cloud of ink covers the escape (cephalopods).
Spraying irritants (bombardier beetles, later skunks).
Harmless species copying dangerous ones.
Clubs and spikes swung at attackers (stegosaurs, ankylosaurs).
Both sexes in one body (snails, worms).
Clones joined into one colony (corals, graptolites).
Leaping and gliding between trees.
Development pauses until conditions improve.
Muscle turned into living batteries that discharge to stun prey (electric eels, torpedo rays).
